questions.stem: Which three groups of living things make up most microorganisms?
options: Bacteria, fungi and protists
Bacteria, viruses and prions
Fungi, mosses and ferns
Protists, insects and worms
questions.explanation: Microorganisms include bacteria, fungi (such as yeasts and moulds) and protists (such as amoebae and many algae). Viruses and prions are not cells and are not usually classed as living organisms.

questions.stem: A microorganism has a nucleus, a cell wall made of chitin and grows as thread-like hyphae on bread. Which group does it belong to?
options: Bacteria
Protists
Plants
Fungi
questions.explanation: Moulds are fungi: they are eukaryotic, have chitin cell walls and grow as networks of hyphae. Bacteria have no nucleus, and plant cell walls are made of cellulose.

questions.stem: Which feature correctly separates bacteria from fungi and protists?
options: Bacteria are always multicellular, never single cells
Bacteria all carry out photosynthesis
Bacteria have no DNA or ribosomes
Bacteria are prokaryotic, with no nucleus
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes, lacking a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, while fungi and protists are eukaryotes. Bacteria are single-celled, only some photosynthesise, and all have DNA and ribosomes.

questions.stem: Which group includes single-celled eukaryotes such as Amoeba and Paramecium?
options: Viruses
Protists
Bacteria
Fungi
questions.explanation: Protists are a diverse group of mostly single-celled eukaryotes, including Amoeba, Paramecium and many algae. Bacteria are prokaryotes, and viruses are not cells.

questions.stem: How do bacteria reproduce, and what kind of reproduction is it?
options: By binary fission, which is asexual
By binary fission, which is sexual
By meiosis, which is asexual
By two cells fusing their DNA, which is sexual
questions.explanation: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission: the cell copies its DNA and splits into two identical cells. Only one parent is involved, so it is asexual reproduction.

questions.stem: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes in ideal conditions. Starting with one cell, how many cells will there be after 2 hours?
questions.explanation: 2 hours is 120 minutes, which is 6 generations of 20 minutes. The number doubles each generation: 2 to the power of 6 is 64. Adding 2 cells each generation, giving 12, mistakes doubling for adding.

questions.stem: Why is the growth of a bacterial population in ideal conditions described as exponential?
options: The population stays constant after the first division
The population doubles in each equal time interval
The population increases by the same number each hour
The population grows quickly and then falls to zero
questions.explanation: In ideal conditions every cell divides in each generation time, so the population doubles at regular intervals. Adding the same number each hour would be linear growth, not exponential.

questions.stem: A bacterial culture in a closed flask of broth grows exponentially for several hours, then its numbers stop increasing and later fall. Which explanation best accounts for the later stages?
options: Temperature rises steadily because bacteria absorb light
Nutrients are used up and wastes build up to toxic levels
The bacteria switch to sexual reproduction and divide more slowly
The bacteria all become spores as soon as growth starts
questions.explanation: In a closed culture, nutrients run out and wastes such as acids accumulate, so the death rate rises to match and then exceed the division rate. Bacteria reproduce asexually, so a switch to sexual reproduction is not the cause.

questions.stem: Which list gives conditions that affect the growth of bacteria?
options: Temperature, nutrients, moisture, pH and removal of wastes
Light intensity, wind speed, altitude and day length only
Soil type, rainfall and the number of predators only
The colour of the container and the time of day
questions.explanation: Different bacteria need specific conditions for growth, including suitable temperature, available nutrients, moisture, pH and the removal of wastes. Light matters only for photosynthetic microbes.

questions.stem: Why does keeping food in a refrigerator at about 4 °C slow its spoilage?
options: Low temperature removes all water from the food by osmosis
Low temperature makes the food too acidic for microbes
Low temperature slows the enzyme reactions microbes need to grow
Low temperature kills all of the bacteria and fungi present in the food
questions.explanation: Cold slows the enzyme-controlled reactions of microorganisms, so they grow and divide much more slowly. Refrigeration does not kill most microbes; they can grow again when the food warms up.

questions.stem: Food safety guidelines in Australia describe 5 °C to 60 °C as the temperature 'danger zone'. Why?
options: Many food-poisoning bacteria grow quickly in this range
All bacteria in food are killed only within this temperature range
Food enzymes stop working completely in this range
Moulds can grow only at temperatures above 60 °C
questions.explanation: Between 5 °C and 60 °C, many bacteria that cause food poisoning can multiply rapidly, so food should be kept colder than 5 °C or hotter than 60 °C. Growth is slow below 5 °C, and high temperatures above 60 °C kill or stop many of them.

questions.stem: A student grows the same bacterium on agar plates at pH 4, 7 and 10, at 37 °C. Colonies grow well at pH 7 but hardly at all at pH 4 or 10. What is the best explanation?
options: Extreme pH provides extra nutrients that slow down cell division
The bacteria at pH 4 and 10 had too much water to reproduce
Temperature was different on each plate, so pH had no effect
Extreme pH changes the shape of the bacterium's enzymes so they work poorly
questions.explanation: Each bacterium has a pH range in which its enzymes keep their shape and work well. At extreme pH the enzymes' active sites change shape, slowing growth. Temperature was held constant at 37 °C, so pH is the variable that explains the result.

questions.stem: In an investigation of temperature on bacterial growth, which set of factors should be held constant?
options: Temperature, number of colonies and colony size
Incubation temperature only, as nothing else affects growth
Number of colonies and the time taken to count them
Type of bacterium, nutrient agar, incubation time and pH
questions.explanation: Temperature is the independent variable and colony number or size is the dependent variable. Other factors that affect growth, such as the strain, nutrient medium, pH and incubation time, must be kept the same for a fair test.

questions.stem: What is the role of decomposers such as many bacteria and fungi in an ecosystem?
options: They prey on living animals and keep their population numbers in check
They fix oxygen gas from the air into organic compounds
They break down dead and waste material, releasing nutrients
They capture light energy to make glucose for consumers
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down dead organisms and wastes, returning nutrients such as nitrogen compounds and carbon dioxide to the soil, water and air. Producers, not decomposers, capture light energy.

questions.stem: If all decomposers were removed from a forest ecosystem, what would happen over time?
options: Plants would grow faster because no nutrients would be lost from the soil
Carbon dioxide levels in the soil would rise sharply
Herbivores would replace decomposers in breaking down wood
Dead material would build up and nutrients would not be recycled
questions.explanation: Without decomposers, dead leaves, wood and bodies would accumulate and the nutrients locked in them would not return to the soil. Plants would eventually run short of mineral nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus.

questions.stem: Decomposing bacteria break down proteins in a dead animal. Which nutrient is returned to the soil in a form plants can eventually use?
options: Oxygen
Glucose
Starch
Nitrogen
questions.explanation: Proteins contain nitrogen. Decomposers release it as ammonium, which other soil bacteria convert to nitrate that plants take up. Glucose and starch are organic compounds that plants make themselves.

questions.stem: Which is a role of bacteria in the human digestive system?
options: Producing vitamin K and helping break down some dietary fibre
Producing hydrochloric acid in the stomach lining
Making the bile that emulsifies dietary fats in the small intestine
Absorbing all glucose into the blood through the villi
questions.explanation: Gut bacteria, mainly in the large intestine, ferment some fibre that human enzymes cannot digest and produce vitamins such as vitamin K. Stomach acid is made by stomach cells, and bile by the liver.

questions.stem: Cattle and sheep cannot make the enzyme cellulase, yet they live on grass. How is this possible?
options: They absorb whole cellulose molecules through the villi
Their saliva contains enzymes that convert cellulose to protein
They obtain all their energy from minerals in the soil
Microorganisms in their gut digest the cellulose for them
questions.explanation: Ruminants house bacteria and other microbes in the rumen that break down cellulose, producing compounds the animal can absorb and use. Cellulose molecules are far too large to be absorbed whole.

questions.stem: Why are phytoplankton important to life on Earth?
options: They decompose dead fish and release oxygen into the water
They absorb oxygen from the air and store it deep in the ocean for animals
They fix nitrogen gas into the protein of all marine animals
They produce a large share of Earth's oxygen by photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Phytoplankton are microscopic photosynthetic organisms, such as diatoms and cyanobacteria, that release oxygen as they photosynthesise. Ocean photosynthesis, mostly by phytoplankton, supplies a large share of Earth's oxygen, and phytoplankton also form the base of marine food webs.

questions.stem: Rising sea temperatures reduce phytoplankton growth in some ocean regions. Which consequence would be expected in those regions?
options: Less carbon dioxide taken up and less food at the base of food webs
More oxygen released because fewer consumers eat phytoplankton
Less nitrogen fixed by fish and more phosphorus in the water
More photosynthesis by zooplankton to replace the phytoplankton
questions.explanation: Phytoplankton take up carbon dioxide in photosynthesis and are the producers on which marine food webs depend, so a decline reduces carbon uptake and food supply. Zooplankton are consumers and cannot photosynthesise.

questions.stem: How are bacteria used to make human insulin for people with diabetes?
options: The human insulin gene is inserted into bacteria, which then make insulin
Bacteria are fed insulin, which they concentrate in their cell walls
Bacteria break down the pancreas tissue of cattle to release the insulin it holds
Bacteria infect human cells and force them to release insulin
questions.explanation: In recombinant DNA technology, the human insulin gene is inserted into a bacterial plasmid and put into bacteria. The bacteria multiply and express the gene, producing human insulin that is then purified.

questions.stem: Bacteria are well suited to producing human proteins such as growth hormone by recombinant DNA technology. Which pair of features best explains this?
options: They contain human chromosomes in their cytoplasm
They reproduce rapidly and the same genetic code is read in all cells
They have a nucleus and reproduce by meiosis
They make all their proteins without ribosomes
questions.explanation: Bacteria multiply quickly by binary fission, and because the genetic code is universal, bacterial ribosomes can translate a human gene into the human protein. Bacteria lack a nucleus and do not undergo meiosis.

questions.stem: For about how long have humans cultured and used microorganisms, for example in making bread and fermented drinks?
options: About 1 million years
About 10 000 years
About 100 years
About 500 years
questions.explanation: Humans have used microorganisms such as yeasts and bacteria in food and drink for about 10 000 years, long before microbes were known. Modern microbiology began only a few hundred years ago, with the microscope.

questions.stem: Yoghurt is made by adding certain bacteria to warm milk. Why does the milk thicken and become sour?
options: The bacteria produce ethanol, which evaporates and thickens the milk
The bacteria release oxygen, which reacts with milk proteins
The bacteria absorb all the water from the milk by osmosis
The bacteria ferment milk sugar to lactic acid, which lowers the pH
questions.explanation: Yoghurt bacteria ferment lactose to lactic acid. The acid gives the sour taste and lowers the pH, which makes milk proteins thicken. Ethanol is produced by yeast fermentation, not by yoghurt bacteria.

questions.stem: What is the main cause of food spoilage?
options: Growth of bacteria and fungi on or in the food
Loss of vitamins as food is exposed to light
Absorption of oxygen from the air by the plastic food packaging
Formation of new minerals in the food
questions.explanation: Most food spoilage is caused by microorganisms, such as bacteria, yeasts and moulds, growing on the food and breaking it down. They change its smell, taste and texture and some produce toxins.

questions.stem: Why is washing hands and using separate boards for raw meat and salad important in a kitchen?
options: It removes water from food so microbes cannot grow
It kills the microbes deep inside the raw meat before it is ever cooked
It stops microbes being transferred to food that will not be cooked
It adds acids to food that slow down microbial growth
questions.explanation: Hygienic practices prevent cross-contamination, the transfer of microbes from hands, raw meat or surfaces to food that is eaten without cooking. Cooking will kill microbes in the meat, but not those carried onto salad.

questions.stem: Jam made with a high concentration of sugar keeps for a long time without spoiling. Why?
options: Sugar coats each microbe so that oxygen cannot reach its cell membrane
Water leaves microbial cells by osmosis, so they cannot grow
Sugar provides so much energy that microbes stop dividing
Sugar raises the pH so high that enzymes are destroyed
questions.explanation: The high sugar concentration outside the microbial cells draws water out of them by osmosis, so they become dehydrated and cannot grow. The same principle explains preserving meat or fish with salt.

questions.stem: Pickling vegetables in vinegar preserves them. Which growth requirement of microorganisms does this method affect?
options: Light
Oxygen
pH
Temperature
questions.explanation: Vinegar contains acetic acid, which lowers the pH below the range most spoilage microbes can tolerate. Their enzymes cannot work properly, so they cannot grow.

questions.stem: How does drying food, such as making dried apricots or beef jerky, preserve it?
options: It raises the temperature so microbes grow faster
It adds nutrients that compete with microbes
It increases the pH so microbes are killed
It removes the water that microbes need to grow
questions.explanation: Microbes need moisture for their metabolism and growth, and drying removes most of the water. Without enough water, bacteria and fungi cannot grow, so the food keeps.

questions.stem: Milk is pasteurised by heating it to about 72 °C for 15 seconds and then cooling it quickly. Why must pasteurised milk still be kept in a refrigerator?
options: Heating kills most but not all microbes, and cold slows those that remain
Heating kills all microbes, but cooling is needed to keep the flavour
Heating adds nutrients that would otherwise attract new microbes
Heating makes milk acidic, and cold is needed to neutralise it
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation kills most microbes, including disease-causing ones, but some heat-resistant microbes survive, and more can enter once the milk is opened. Refrigeration slows their growth. Full sterilisation would need higher temperatures.

questions.stem: Which preservation method is correctly matched with the reason it works?
options: Freezing: ice crystals kill every microbe in the food
Salting: salt raises the pH so enzymes in microbes stop working
Smoking: smoke adds water that dilutes microbial enzymes
Canning: heat kills microbes and the sealed can stops new ones entering
questions.explanation: Canning heats food to kill microbes and then seals it, preventing recontamination. Freezing stops growth but does not kill all microbes, and salting works by drawing water out of microbes by osmosis, not by changing pH.

questions.stem: Which method preserves food by destroying microorganisms rather than just slowing their growth?
options: Heating, as in canning or pasteurising
Refrigerating at about 4 °C
Freezing at about minus 18 °C
Storing food in a sealed dark cupboard for weeks
questions.explanation: High temperatures kill microorganisms by denaturing their proteins. Refrigeration and freezing slow or stop growth but most microbes survive, and darkness does not affect most food-spoilage microbes.

questions.stem: Antibiotic discs are placed on an agar plate spread with bacteria. After incubation, disc X has a clear zone 18 mm wide and disc Y has one 6 mm wide. What can be concluded?
options: Both antibiotics speed up the growth of the bacterium
Antibiotic X inhibited the growth of this bacterium more than Y
Antibiotic Y inhibited the growth of this bacterium more than X
Neither antibiotic had any effect on this bacterium
questions.explanation: A clear zone shows where bacteria could not grow, so a wider zone means the antibiotic inhibited this bacterium more strongly. The result applies to this bacterium under these conditions, and repeat trials would improve reliability.

questions.stem: The dry mass of a bacterial sample is recorded as 0.004050 g. How many significant figures does this value have?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point and are not significant, so counting starts at 4. The digits 4, 0, 5 and the final 0 are all significant, because a trailing zero after the decimal point shows measured precision.

questions.stem: A student calculates a bacterial population of 23 456 cells per mL. What is this value rounded to three significant figures?
options: 23 500 cells per mL
23 400 cells per mL
234 cells per mL
23 460 cells per mL
questions.explanation: The first three significant figures are 2, 3 and 4, and the next digit is 5, so the 4 rounds up to 5, giving 23 500. Zeros hold the place value, so the number is not shortened to 234.

questions.stem: Three repeat measurements of a zone of inhibition are 12.3 mm, 12.5 mm and 12.6 mm. What mean should be reported?
options: 12 mm
questions.explanation: The mean is 37.4 / 3 = 12.466..., but each measurement has three significant figures (to 0.1 mm), so the mean should be given to the same precision, 12.5 mm. Extra digits suggest more precision than the measurements had.

questions.stem: A student claims a hand sanitiser 'kills 99.9% of bacteria' after testing it on one plate of one bacterial species. Why is this conclusion limited?
options: Bacteria cannot be counted, so no percentage can be found
The claim is valid because one plate contains millions of cells
One trial on one species cannot show the effect on all bacteria
Hand sanitisers cannot be tested on agar plates at all
questions.explanation: A single trial gives no measure of reliability, and testing one species cannot support a claim about all bacteria. Repeat trials with several species and a control plate would be needed. Many cells on one plate does not replace repetition or variety.
